lesson.content:
## What it is
Network topologies describe the physical or logical arrangement of devices in a network. [p. 2]
## Real-life analogy
Imagine a race where all runners are connected by a single rope. If the rope breaks, the whole race stops. [p. 2]
## How it works
1. **Bus**: All devices are connected to a single cable, like a single rope in a race. If the cable breaks, the whole network stops. [p. 2]
2. **Star**: Each device is connected to a central hub or switch, like runners in a relay race where each runner has a separate connection. Adding a device requires connecting it to the hub, which can be complex. [p. 2]
3. **Ring**: Devices are connected in a circular pattern, like a circle of runners. If one device or link breaks, the entire network stops. [p. 2]
4. **Mesh**: Every device has a dedicated connection to every other device, like a network where each device is connected to every other device directly. This is very reliable but requires a lot of connections. [p. 2]
5. **Hybrid**: A combination of two or more topologies, like a hybrid car that uses different types of engines. It is flexible but complex to design. [p. 2]
## Key terms
- **Bus**: All devices share one cable, easy to install, but a single point of failure. [p. 2]
- **Star**: Devices connect to a central hub, easy to add devices, but one failure can affect the whole network. [p. 2]
- **Ring**: Devices form a circle, no collisions, but one failure can break the network. [p. 2]
- **Mesh**: Every device has a dedicated connection, very reliable, but expensive and requires a lot of cabling. [p. 2]
- **Hybrid**: Combination of two or more topologies, flexible but complex to design. [p. 2]
## Example
Consider a school network where each classroom is connected to a central hub. If the hub fails, the whole school network stops working. [p. 2]
## What to draw in the exam
No diagram needed. [p. 2]
## Exam tip
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of each topology in the context of a network setup. [p. 2]
